analysis.one_liner: Forgives federal water-project debts and transfers federal facilities to Central Valley irrigation districts.
analysis.headline: A bill to forgive San Luis Unit water contractors' federal repayment debts died in committee without a single cosponsor or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: California's San Luis Unit is a federal irrigation project in the Central Valley whose water contractors — farm districts, most notably the Westlands area — owe the federal government repayment for building the project, and the project has an unresolved drainage-water problem. This bill, H.R. 5217, would suspend those repayment obligations, give the districts credits against future costs, relieve them of capital repayment under their water contracts, and transfer title of federal facilities and property to the districts (S2, S3). It was introduced on May 12, 2016 by Rep. Jim Costa (D-CA), referred to the House Natural Resources Committee and then its Water, Power and Oceans Subcommittee, and received no further action before the 114th Congress ended (S1, S5). No other member signed on as a cosponsor (S4).
analysis.who_benefits: The San Luis Unit irrigation contractors — the farm water districts that receive project water — gain the most: their federal capital repayment obligations would be suspended and largely relieved, they would receive credits against future operation and maintenance costs owed to the United States, and they would take title to federal facilities and real property used to deliver their water (S2, S3). Taxpayers currently on the hook for the unit's unresolved drainage problem would also gain certainty, but the primary beneficiaries are the water districts, whose debts and assets would be settled in their favor.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Central Valley irrigation districts holding federal water contracts

how_it_helps.text: The bill suspends each San Luis Unit Contractor's capital repayment obligation and payments under its water service contracts and the April 1, 1965 repayment contract with the United States, then relieves the contractors of capital repayment obligations under specified water service contracts once new contracts are executed.
Each Northerly and Southerly San Luis Unit District would receive a credit against future operation and maintenance costs payable to the United States.
The bill requires Interior to transfer title to specified federal facilities, equipment, and real property interests to the San Luis Unit Contractors upon execution of the new repayment contracts.
The bill would resolve, on federal terms set by this bill, the contractors' exposure tied to the unit's drainage problem, which has gone unresolved since the project was built.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers pay. Debt repayment obligations owed to the United States would be forgiven or credited, federal facilities and real property would be transferred to the districts, and any drainage fix costing $5 million or more would be repaid under reclamation law — costs borne by the Treasury rather than fully by the water users who received the benefit of the project (S2, S3).
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers, through forgiven debts and transferred assets

drawbacks.text: Forgiving capital repayment obligations and handing federal facilities to the districts shifts the cost of a federally built irrigation project away from the water users who benefit from it and onto the general taxpayer.
The credit against future operation and maintenance costs directly reduces what the districts pay the United States for running the system.
Because the bill was never marked up, debated, or scored in committee, there is no official estimate of what the debt relief and asset transfers would cost taxpayers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would have settled a decades-old dispute that burdens both the districts and the federal government, and ending drainage uncertainty has real value for the farm communities involved. But the settlement's terms run one way: the districts' repayment debts would be suspended and largely relieved, they would get credits against what they owe, and they would receive title to federal facilities and land. The costs of those concessions would fall on the Treasury — that is, on taxpayers everywhere — with no offsetting public benefit specified in the bill itself.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the House Natural Resources Committee and its Water, Power and Oceans Subcommittee until the Congress ended, never getting a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Jim Costa introduced the San Luis Unit Drainage Resolution Act in the House on May 12, 2016.
The bill was referred the same day to the House Committee on Natural Resources, and on May 16, 2016 was referred within the committee to the Subcommittee on Water, Power and Oceans.
The committee never reported the bill, and the House never voted on it before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017, so the bill died and would have had to be reintroduced to move again.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal taxpayers and the general public are better off that the bill died, since its debt forgiveness, credits, and federal asset transfers to the irrigation districts were never enacted; the water districts remain in the same position they were in before it was introduced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Taxpayers; the districts' debts and asset transfer were never enacted

for.name: Rep. Jim Costa
for.role: Sponsor (D-CA), whose Central Valley district includes San Luis Unit communities
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the House Natural Resources Committee; recruited no cosponsors.

against.name: House Natural Resources Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; its chair controls whether the bill ever gets a hearing or markup
against.what_they_did: Took no further action on the bill after referral to the Water, Power and Oceans Subcommittee, and never reported it to the House.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no party split is on record; it had a single Democratic sponsor, no cosponsors of either party, and no committee action.

industries.industry: Irrigated agriculture / Central Valley water districts
industries.note: The bill's direct beneficiaries: the San Luis Unit water contractors would have their federal capital repayment debts suspended and largely relieved, receive credits against what they owe, and take title to federal facilities and land that serve their farms. Their interest in this bill runs against the general taxpayer's, since the costs shift to the Treasury.

Not an industry but the paying party: forgiving repayment obligations, crediting future operation and maintenance costs, and transferring federal facilities and property all reduce what returns to the Treasury from a federal reclamation project.
